title: Nothing new
hookLine: there is no new thing under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:9)
tomorrow: what happens when you throw your bread on the water?

lines: THE SAME WORRIES, WORD FOR WORD.
NO NEW THING UNDER THE SUN.
cards: Read a parent's letters from when they were your age, or an old diary, and there's a jolt: the same worries, almost word for word. Is that bad news, or a relief? The Preacher stands outside and watches.
The sun rises, sets, and hurries back to where it rose. The wind goes south, turns north, circles round. "All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full."
Then he says it: "there is no new thing under the sun."

teach.b: On its own, that sounds tired. But look at the line just before the sun: "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever." The people change.
The ground holds. So Qoheleth's nothing new cuts two ways.
It humbles: your crisis isn't the first, and the book says plainly that former things aren't remembered. And it steadies: whatever you're walking through, others walked this ground and it held them.
Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: MARCUS: SEEN THE PRESENT, SEEN ALL.
teach.b: Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor and Stoic, wrote in his private notebook that whoever has seen the present has seen everything, all that has been and all that will be, since all things are of one kind and one form.
Same sun, two windows. And the honest difference: Marcus finds his peace in the reason that runs through nature, and in doing his duty inside it.
Qoheleth's book ends somewhere else: "Fear God, and keep his commandments," and meanwhile eat your bread as God's gift. Neither is the other in disguise.
The teaching, plainly: in Ecclesiastes, nothing new is a humbling truth and a comfort at once, because the earth that outlasts you also held everyone before you.

how: Ecclesiastes is read as wisdom literature in Jewish and Christian tradition; its 'under the sun' passages sit within a book that closes on the call to fear God and keep the commandments. Marcus Aurelius's Meditations voices a similar view of the world's repeating patterns.

o: everything was invented long ago by the ancients
the world is boring and not worth exploring
what has been will be: humbling, and a comfort too

games.q: the sun, the rivers and a neighbor: tap the pairs.
p: run to a sea that's never full
seen the present, seen it all

s: 'nothing new under the sun' is only a complaint
next to it: generations go, but the earth abides. it humbles and it steadies.
a Roman emperor wrote something close to it
Marcus Aurelius: whoever has seen the present has seen all things.
Marcus Aurelius and Ecclesiastes end in the same place
Marcus rests in nature's reason and duty; Ecclesiastes ends: fear God, and keep his commandments.

games.q: a friend starting a first job says, 'everyone's done this before me. what's the point?' what's the Ecclesiastes answer?
o: that's the comfort: generations walked this way and the ground held. walk it your way.
she's right: if it's nothing new, nothing she does there can matter.
she should find something nobody has ever done, or it's all hevel.
games.why: Qoheleth sets 'no new thing under the sun' beside 'the earth abideth for ever': the old path is humbling and steadying at once.

practice: Think of one thing you do that people before you did too: a recipe, a song, the way you fold laundry, even a worry. Hold the people who did it before you in mind, one generation behind another.
For a minute, let the old pattern carry you, instead of you carrying it.

wordCard.voice: Nothing new: the sun, the wind and the rivers going round, and the earth holding still under all of it.

orig.note: Hebrew: under the sun, Qoheleth's phrase for life as we see it from here.

carryVoice: Here's the line: nothing new; someone stood exactly here before, and the ground held. Back tomorrow.
